claims.text: An intermediate Al addition of approximately 10–20 at.% promotes nanoscale chemical heterogeneity in lightweight HEAs.
Nanoscale Al segregation leads to in situ formation of a coherent, protective oxide scale composed primarily of Al2O3 during high-temperature exposure.
Nanoscale chemical segregation strengthens the alloy through dislocation pinning.
A processed hierarchical nanostructure can simultaneously provide low density, high strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The baseline alloy with less than 3 at.% Al lacks the nanoscale chemical heterogeneity needed to form a coherent protective oxide scale.
Controlled homogenization and thermal processing of an alloy containing approximately 15 at.% Al promotes nanoscale Al segregation and Al-rich cluster formation.
Al-rich domains can coexist discretely within a refractory alloy matrix.
Al-rich domains act as nucleation sites for a coherent, self-passivating Al2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure.
Moderate Al content creates local chemical-potential fluctuations that drive nanoscale Al clustering during thermal treatment.
At high temperature, Al-rich clusters oxidize rapidly to produce a continuous and coherent Al2O3 layer.
A continuous Al2O3 layer retards subsequent oxidation and corrosion.
Substitution of heavier elements with approximately 15 at.% Al reduces alloy density relative to the low-Al baseline.
The approximately 15 at.% Al alloy will retain or improve yield strength relative to the low-Al baseline because nanoscale heterogeneity impedes dislocation motion.
The approximately 15 at.% Al alloy will have lower corrosion current density or longer salt-spray endurance than the low-Al baseline.
At 900°C in air, the approximately 15 at.% Al alloy will form a thinner, more adherent Al2O3 scale than the low-Al baseline.
Al contents substantially below or above approximately 10–20 at.% will prevent the proposed combination of oxide protection and mechanical strength.
Insufficient Al provides too few sites for protective oxide formation.
Excessive Al can cause deleterious phase separation that reduces strength.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that the hypothesis ceases to hold when processing conditions 'preserve the segregated Al-rich domains,' whereas the conditions and structural-mediator fields require preservation of those domains. This appears to be a wording error; dissolution or prevention of the domains would be the coherent boundary.

The intervention requires substituting Al for a portion of other elements, but the comparison design says that all other elements are kept identical. In normalized atomic-percent compositions, increasing Al from below 3 at.% to about 15 at.% necessarily decreases at least one other elemental fraction.
